sample_n: 1264 (Bygdøy) / 1370 (Romeriksåsen) panel respondents interviewed at t1 and t2
exposure: change in aircraft noise from the 1998 relocation of Norway's main airport; old airport closed leaving high-altitude overflights and helicopters while the new airport was expanded
behaviour_measure: visitor vs non-visitor status at t2; frequency of use of the area in the past three months; aircraft noise reported as a reason for not visiting
measurement_method: self-report (telephone interview panel before and after the change)
key_finding: Changed aircraft noise exposure influenced individual choices to use the local outdoor recreational areas - with noise reported as a reason for non-use - but use was largely stable and also fluctuated for reasons unrelated to noise (magnitudes not in excerpt).

sample_n: NR (five consecutive working days of covert video observation of a campus concourse)
exposure: three instrumental music excerpts (classical / jazz / ambient electronic) vs a no-music control played over two loudspeakers; background level profiled with ten microphones and SPL propagation simulated as homogeneous across the observation area
behaviour_measure: number of people stopping in the observation area; duration of stay in seconds coded from a BORIS ethogram
key_finding: The presence of music had no effect on the number of people stopping but a statistically significant positive effect on the duration of stay of those who stopped (magnitude not in excerpt).

setting: campus (Alnarp rehabilitation garden - restricted-access therapeutic garden)
design: survey (qualitative semi-structured interviews analysed with Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis)
exposure: garden soundscape categorised as natural (birdsong / running water / rustling vegetation) technological and human sounds; motorway E6 about 0.6 km east with an LAeq 24h noise map for the site
behaviour_measure: self-reported garden usage in relation to sound (cross-theme dimension: sound in relation to garden usage) alongside overall perception and susceptibility to sound
key_finding: Natural sounds were experienced as part of a pleasant quiet recovery-supporting experience while technological sounds disturbed and human sounds varied with loudness and social context; sound also influenced how patients used the garden (qualitative - no magnitude reported).

exposure: headphone playback during a 1.8 km urban walk: traffic noise track at mean 53 dBA vs forest birdsong track at mean 56 dBA vs a no-sound control; route traffic noise about Lday 55-60 dBA in sections 1-4 and 50-55 dBA in sections 5-7
behaviour_measure: walking speed (m/s) across seven marked sections of the route
measurement_method: sensor-GPS-video (waist-worn video camera used to time marked section crossings)
key_finding: Participants listening to traffic noise walked significantly faster than both the forest-birdsong and the control participants while birdsong listeners walked slightly slower than controls (not significant).

setting: street (two commercial pedestrian streets - Kuan Alley and Central Avenue)
design: mixed (field-observation of crowds + acoustic measurement + questionnaire)
sample_n: 26 survey days over two seasons; questionnaire respondent count NR (about 40% male / 60% female)
exposure: contextual factors of the acoustic environment - shop openness (semi-open vs closed) season (summer vs winter) and commercial function zone (dining with hawking / shopping with pop background music at 95-100 bpm / performance with live instrumental music)
behaviour_measure: number of talkers counted every 30 s from video of the survey zone; crowd density (persons/m2) measured photographically with a drone
measurement_method: sensor-GPS-video and observation (drone photography + video counting) plus self-report questionnaire for acoustic comfort
key_finding: Crowd and talking behaviour shaped the soundscape - a 0.1 persons/m2 rise in crowd density raised sound pressure level by 1.3 dBA in winter and 2.2 dBA in summer - and the number of talkers rose with density (higher in Central Avenue) while acoustic comfort declined in Kuan Alley and was parabolic in Central Avenue.
effect_stats: crowd density +0.1 persons/m2 -> SPL +1.3 dBA (winter) and +2.2 dBA (summer); Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality test and t-tests at p<0.01 and p<0.05

setting: square (100 m x 70 m urban leisure square in Harbin)
sample_n: NR (on-site crowd observation; crowd density under 0.05 persons/m2)
exposure: familiar pop song 'Free to Fly' at 120 bpm reproduced through a concealed loudspeaker at 88-90 dBA cyclically alternated with silence; background level 56.7 dBA and 88.3 dBA at 2 m from the source
behaviour_measure: path and speed of passing-by behaviour; area perimeter and speed of walking-around paths; crowd density of sitting behaviour by distance from the sound source
measurement_method: observation (on-site behavioural observation) combined with grid sound level measurement
key_finding: Music centralised passing-by paths (8.3% of people walked near the square edge without music vs 0% with music) reduced the mean area and perimeter of walking-around paths slowed walking-around speed by 0.296 m/s and concentrated sitting nearer the sound source while passing-by speed was unchanged.
effect_stats: passing-by near edge 8.3% (no music) vs 0% (music); walking-around mean speed 0.296 m/s slower with music

setting: park (three public spaces in Amsterdam including two traditional urban parks)
design: mixed (behavioural mapping observation + on-site questionnaire + spatial analysis)
sample_n: NR (park users approached on site; count not in excerpt)
exposure: everyday in-situ soundscapes of three Amsterdam public spaces with no intervention; users' ranked soundscape evaluations and free-response descriptions of what they heard
behaviour_measure: observable activity categories and their locations recorded by non-intrusive behavioural mapping; level of social interaction of the activity (solitary vs socially interactive)
measurement_method: observation (behavioural mapping) plus self-report (on-site questionnaire with ranked evaluations and open-ended justifications)
key_finding: Socially interactive users rated their soundscapes as more suitable and less disruptive for their activity than solitary users - so the social level of the ongoing activity shapes soundscape evaluation (magnitudes not in excerpt).

setting: park (four urban green spaces in Rostock)
exposure: everyday soundscape of green spaces designated quiet areas (Lden < 50 dB) characterised by 12 sounds including street traffic motorcycle noise bird song water sound and tree rustling
behaviour_measure: length of stay (<1 h / 1-3 h / >3 h); visit frequency; five visit motivations
key_finding: Among the social/demographic/behavioural factors length of stay was the one most associated with soundscape experience (especially perception of street traffic sound and bird song) and all five visit motivations were positively related to overall soundscape preference with 'Enjoy a quiet environment' the strongest (rho = 0.323).
effect_stats: Spearman rho = 0.323 for 'Enjoy a quiet environment' vs overall soundscape preference (other coefficients in tables not in excerpt)

setting: park (pocket park - Parc du Portugal Montreal)
design: mixed (soundscape intervention evaluated with questionnaires interviews behavioural observation and acoustic monitoring)
sample_n: NR (park users and non-users across five project phases; counts not in excerpt)
exposure: Musikiosk - an unsupervised gazebo installation letting park users play their own audio content over publicly provided speakers during summer 2015
behaviour_measure: behavioural observations of park use; activity categorisation before vs after installation; lingering interaction and sharing behaviours
measurement_method: observation (behavioural observation) plus self-report (questionnaires and interviews) plus acoustic monitoring
key_finding: The user-controlled music installation increased social interaction and lingering behaviours and animated an underused section of the park without displacing existing users while perceived soundscape calmness and appropriateness were not affected.
